chapters.name: Chapter 1: Who buys and what you offer

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Describing your ideal customer
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short, specific description of the customer you most want more of.
This lesson builds toward: Given what you see with your best customers, you will write a short, specific description of your ideal customer with AI help, in three sentences that say who they are, what they need and why they choose you.
You cannot sell well to everyone. Think of your best customers: the ones who come back, spend well and send friends. What do they have in common?
Write three sentences: who they are, what they need, and what makes them choose you. Example for a West African restaurant: "Office workers within two miles who want a filling lunch under $15. They are busy and order on their phones. They choose us for big portions and fast pickup."
AI can help you think: "Here is what I know about my best customers. What questions should I ask myself to describe them better?" Use what you see in your shop, not guesses about groups of people.
Step by step:
- Picture your five best customers.
- Write what they have in common.
- Write three sentences: who, what they need, why you.
- Ask AI for questions that sharpen it.
Words to know:
- Ideal customer: the kind of customer who is the best fit for your business.
- Repeat customer: someone who buys from you more than once.
Try it now: Write your ideal customer in three sentences. Ask an AI assistant for five questions to make it sharper, answer them, and rewrite your three sentences.
You can now describe the customer you most want more of in three clear sentences.

check.q: Where should your ideal customer description come from?
options: What you see with your real best customers
A guess about everyone in town
check.why: Your real best customers show who to look for.

check.q: Your description says "everyone who likes food". What would you do?
options: Keep it because it includes more people
Ask AI for sharpening questions and make it specific
check.why: A specific description helps you reach the right people.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing an offer that makes sense
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create one clear, honest offer with a price, a reason to act and an end date.
This lesson builds toward: Given offer ideas from AI, you will create one clear, honest offer, with what, price, reason to act and end date, and a profit worked out on paper.
An offer is what you are selling, at what price, and why someone should buy now. Good offers are simple: "Lunch combo: rice, stew and drink, $13, weekdays 11 to 2 through June 30."
Ask AI to brainstorm, then you choose: "I run a mobile detailing service. My ideal customer is busy parents. Give me five offer ideas for the spring that keep my profit." Check the math yourself: a discount that loses money on every sale is not growth.
Keep it honest. Say the real price, the real end date and any limits. Do not call it a sale if it is your normal price.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for five offer ideas for your ideal customer.
- Pick one and work out your cost and profit.
- Write it with what, price, reason to act and end date.
- Check it is honest and clear.
Words to know:
- Offer: what you sell, the price and the reason to buy now.
- Profit: money left after you pay your costs.
- Margin: the share of the price that is profit.
Try it now: Ask AI for five offer ideas for your ideal customer. Pick one, work out your cost and profit on paper, and write the offer in one sentence with an end date.
You can now write a clear, honest offer that still makes a profit.

check.q: What does a clear offer include?
options: What, price, reason to act and end date
A promise that it never ends
check.why: These parts make an offer easy to understand and act on.

check.q: AI suggests half off everything for a month. What would you do first?
options: Ask customers if they like it
Work out on paper whether you still make a profit
check.why: An offer must still leave money after costs.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Starting a simple customer list
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a simple customer list in a spreadsheet, with permission to contact.
This lesson builds toward: Using a spreadsheet, you will set up a customer list that records permission to contact, with a column for agreement and date, a sign-up method, and no real customer data in AI.
Your customer list is your most valuable sales tool. It can be a spreadsheet with columns like First name, How to contact (email or phone), Agreed to messages (yes/no and date), Last visit, What they bought, and Notes.
Only add people who gave you their details and agreed to hear from you: a sign-up sheet at the counter, a QR code to a form, or a checkbox in your booking tool. Write down when and how they agreed.
Keep the list private and safe: a password on the file or account, shared only with staff who need it. Do not paste the list into AI tools. If you want AI help, describe the columns or use made-up sample rows.
Step by step:
- Make a spreadsheet with the columns above.
- Add a sign-up method: counter sheet, QR form or booking checkbox.
- Record when and how each person agreed.
- Protect the file and keep it out of AI tools.
Words to know:
- Customer list: a record of customers who agreed to hear from you.
- Opt in: when a person agrees to receive your messages.
- CRM: customer relationship management: software or a sheet for tracking customers.
Try it now: Make your customer list sheet with the six columns. Add three made-up sample rows, then write how real customers will sign up (counter sheet, QR form or booking checkbox).
You can now set up a private customer list with a record of permission to contact.

check.q: Who belongs on your customer list?
options: People who agreed to hear from you
Anyone whose number you can find
check.why: Only people who said yes to hearing from you go on the list.

check.q: You want AI to help design your customer list sheet. What would you share?
options: The column names or made-up sample rows
check.why: Column names or sample rows get help without sharing real customer data.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing follow-ups that follow the rules
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a three-message follow-up sequence and make marketing emails follow CAN-SPAM.
This lesson builds toward: Given CAN-SPAM and the texting rules, you will write a three-message follow-up sequence with AI help, with a postal address and unsubscribe line on any marketing email, and texts only with clear permission.
Most sales come from following up. A simple sequence: (1) thank you after a visit, (2) a reminder or tip a week later, (3) your offer with its end date. Ask AI: "Write three short follow-up emails for my salon in my brand voice. Use [first name]."
Marketing emails in the US must follow the CAN-SPAM Act. The FTC's guide says: use honest From and subject lines, make clear it is an ad, include a valid postal address, give a clear way to unsubscribe, and honor unsubscribe requests within 10 business days.
Marketing texts have their own federal rules (the TCPA, enforced by the FCC), and they generally need the customer's clear permission. Before you send marketing texts, check the rules at fcc.gov or ask a professional, and use a texting tool that handles opt-outs.
Step by step:
- Plan three messages: thanks, reminder or tip, offer.
- Ask AI to draft them with [first name] blanks.
- Add your postal address and an unsubscribe line to marketing emails.
- Honor unsubscribes quickly.
- Check texting rules before sending marketing texts.
Words to know:
- Follow-up sequence: a planned series of messages sent after a customer's visit or sign-up.
- CAN-SPAM: the US law with rules for commercial email.
- Unsubscribe: a way for people to stop getting your messages.
Official sources:
- FTC: CAN-SPAM Act, A Compliance Guide for Business
Try it now: Ask AI to draft your three-message follow-up sequence with [first name]. Add your postal address and an unsubscribe line to the offer email.
You can now write a follow-up sequence and make marketing emails meet the CAN-SPAM basics.

check.q: What must every US marketing email include under CAN-SPAM?
options: A valid postal address and a way to unsubscribe
check.why: CAN-SPAM requires a postal address and a way to unsubscribe.

check.q: You want to send marketing texts about your offer. What would you do first?
options: Use a bought list of numbers
Get clear permission and check the federal texting rules
check.why: Marketing texts have their own federal rules and need clear permission.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Reading your sales numbers with AI help
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Track a few sales numbers weekly and use AI to help spot patterns.
This lesson builds toward: Given four weeks of sales numbers, you will track your sales numbers in a table and check AI's patterns, with formulas for totals, customer names removed and at least one pattern confirmed in the sheet.
You only need a few numbers: sales per day, number of customers, average sale (sales divided by customers), your best-selling items, and how many people used your offer.
Keep them in a spreadsheet by week. Let the spreadsheet do the math. Then you can paste the weekly totals (no customer names) into an AI assistant and ask: "Here are 6 weeks of numbers for my bakery. What patterns do you see? What should I check?"
Treat AI's ideas as questions, not answers. If it says "Saturdays are slow", look at your own sheet to confirm, and think about why: weather, an event, a staff change.
Step by step:
- Track sales, customers, average sale, best sellers and offer use each week.
- Let formulas do the totals.
- Paste weekly totals (no names) into AI and ask for patterns.
- Confirm each pattern in your sheet.
Words to know:
- Average sale: total sales divided by the number of customers.
- Pattern: something that happens again and again in your numbers.
Try it now: Make a weekly tracking table with the five numbers. Fill in sample or real numbers for four weeks and ask AI what patterns it sees. Confirm one in your sheet.
You can now track key sales numbers and use AI to help spot patterns you then confirm.

check.q: How do you work out your average sale?
options: Sales divided by number of customers
check.why: Average sale is total sales divided by the number of customers.

check.q: You want AI to look at your weekly sales table. What would you do first?
options: Add customer names so it knows more
Paste it in as it is
check.why: Customer names stay out of AI tools.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your 30-day sales plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Put your customer, offer, list, follow-ups and tracking into one 30-day plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given your customer, offer, list, follow-ups and tracking, you will write a one-page 30-day sales plan, fitted to your real hours, with weekly numbers to check and a day-30 review.
A plan turns ideas into action. Week 1: set up your customer list and sign-up. Week 2: launch your offer and send the thank-you message. Week 3: send the reminder and post the offer. Week 4: send the last call before the end date, then review your numbers.
Ask AI to turn your notes into a calendar with tasks for each week. Keep it realistic for your hours.
At the end, compare your numbers to the month before. Keep what worked, drop what did not, and plan the next 30 days.
Step by step:
- Gather your ideal customer, offer, list setup, follow-ups and tracking table.
- Ask AI to make a four-week task calendar.
- Fit tasks to your real hours.
- Review results at day 30.
Words to know:
- Sales plan: a written plan of what you will do to sell more, and when.
- Review: looking back at results to decide what to keep or change.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page 30-day sales plan with ideal customer, offer, list, three-message sequence and tracking table. Ask AI to turn it into a weekly task calendar.
You can now plan, run and review a 30-day sales push for your business.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Ideal customer Vague, such as "everyone". Three specific sentences: who, what they need and why you. Based on real best customers and sharpened with AI's questions. Offer Missing a price or end date, or loses money. One clear, honest offer with price, reason to act and end date. Profit is worked out and written next to it. Customer list No permission column, or no sign-up method. Says where the list lives and how people joined it, with permission recorded. Notes how the list is protected and kept out of AI tools. Follow-up sequence Fewer than three messages, or a marketing email missing the address or unsubscribe line. Three messages, with address and unsubscribe line on marketing email. Notes the permission and rules needed before any marketing text. Tracking table No table or no weekly numbers. A table with the numbers to check each week, using formulas. Includes a day-30 review to keep what worked. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is Week 1 of the 30-day plan for?
options: Setting up the list and sign-up
check.why: The first week sets up the list and how people join it.

check.q: Your 30-day plan needs more hours than you have. What would you do?
options: Keep it and work all night
Ask AI to do the selling
Cut it back to fit your real hours
check.why: A plan that fits your hours is one you can actually do.
